## 

**Jonathan Nally:** In science there are lots of ways in which your life's work can be recognised. There are prizes and awards galore, important positions to be held, theories to be founded, species can be named after you, and impressive bricks and mortar facilities can be named in your honour. But for the high-achiever who has everything, it's a must to be immortalised in the sky. For instance, you can get a crater or a mountain on another planet named after you.

But when I say that you can do it, I really mean that someone else can propose your name. You can't do it because you have to have been dead for at least three years, or if you are a political figure you have to have been dead for over 200 years. And sorry, military and religious figures are out. And you must have been 'a person of high and enduring international standing'. Well, that rules me out.

But that does leave a lot of distinguished, deceased people, and there are thousands of them now commemorated on bodies in the Solar System. In fact just recently 19 more had lunar craters named after them. Most of these new ones are Nobel Prize winners. There are chemists like Carl Bosch, Fritz Haber and Victor Grignard. There are medical researchers like Theodor Kocher, who studied the thyroid, and Bernardo Houssay, the Argentinean who worked on pituitary hormones. Astronomers and even a 15th century Polish cartographer are in there too.

But the one that really caught my eye was none other than our very own Howard Walter Florey. Florey, of course, is famous for turning an obscure substance called penicillin into a new medicine during World War Two. In recognition of his work, he was knighted in 1944, jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in 1945, and promoted to Baron in 1965. Post-war he became provost of Queen's College, Oxford, and later Chancellor of the ANU. The Howard Florey Institute in Melbourne is named in his honour, and his face was on the $50 note for many years. Prime Minister Menzies called him the 'most important man ever born in Australia'.

So why was his nationality given as British, not Australian? This was just not right. Back in Florey's day of course most Australians also considered themselves to be British. That's no longer the case, of course, but even so, while he might have been a citizen of the British Empire, his nationality definitely was Australian.

Something had to be done, so I fired off an email to the US Geological Survey, the body that maintains the master list of Solar System names. I told them that there would be trouble from down this way unless Florey's proper nationality was instated. Well, I received a nice reply pointing out that the official source documents they use list Florey as being British, apparently based on where he did the work that led to his Nobel Prize. But they did at least agree to amend the listing to 'Australian-born British pathologist'.

So, that's a partial victory at least. If you want to take it any further, you're welcome to contact me and I can put you in touch with the Maintainers of the Master List of Mixed-up Moon Monikers. Florey of course was the man who turned penicillin into a mass-produced medicine during World War Two, leading to a Noble Prize in 1945.

Well, Florey isn't the only Aussie on the Moon. According to the US Geological Survey's master list of Solar System names, there are four other Aussies immortalised on the lunar surface, or maybe five, or is it six, or even seven. The four definites are 19th and 20th century astronomers John Tebbutt, Joe Pawsey, Colin Gum and Arthur Hogg, all of whom now have craters named after them.

The fifth belongs to Antarctic explorer Douglas Mawson, who has a 132-kilometre-long ridge named after him. Although he was born in Britain, Mawson lived in Australia from the age of two.

The sixth is Sir Thomas Brisbane. Born in England, he joined the army in 1789 and served under the Duke of Wellington before leaving for Australia in 1821 to become Governor of New South Wales. He was also an astronomer and he made important contributions to the study of the southern skies. So he's sort of an honorary Aussie.

And as for the seventh...well, the list shows a crater named after Sir William Henry Bragg, a pioneer of X-ray studies and inventor of the X-ray spectrometer. Although he spent a lot of his working life in Australia and therefore can also be considered an honorary Aussie, he was actually British by birth too. So I wonder if they actually mean his son, Sir William Lawrence Bragg, who was born in Adelaide.

At the age of five, Bill junior fell off his bike and his famous dad used the then-new X-ray technique to examine his son's broken arm; its first surgical use in this country. Bragg junior followed his father into science, and together they hold the distinction of being the only father and son team to win the Nobel Prize, in 1915 for their X-ray studies of crystal structure. Bragg junior was only 25, and is still the youngest Nobel laureate.

So, whose name adorns that crater, the old Bill or the young Bill? The world needs to know. So another email was sent to the US Geological Survey, and hopefully we'll soon know if that lunar depression is actually named for the father, the son, or is the hole of both.

**Robyn Williams:** I think it's the son, Lawrence Bragg. Anyway, the Bragg Initiative bringing science to the Australian public starts in Adelaide in October this year.

# **IAU Formally Adopts Name Haskin Crater**

*January 28, 2009  
 Source: LunarWiki/Chuck Wood*

When Riccioli gave names to lunar craters in 1651, many were for his contemporaries, scholars he knew. This is happening again, with the recent addition of Ryder Crater in 2006 (named after Graham Ryder, 1949–2002) and now Haskin Crater, named in honor of Larry Haskin. Haskin died in 2005 of myelofibrosis, a bone marrow disease for which he had been treated for more than 15 years. He was 70 years old.

Haskin was a highly regarded lunar geochemist who was a major contributor to the Lunar and Planetary Science Conference for decades until his death in 2005. In the 1960s, his research helped establish the field of rare-earth-element geochemistry. In 1969, he was one of the researchers to study the first lunar samples returned by the Apollo 11 mission.

In 1973 he became Chief of the Planetary and Earth Sciences Division at the NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston. One of his major accomplishments at JSC was to begin the task of securing the lunar sample collection for future researchers by building a safer, modern curatorial facility. Haskin continued his lunar research until his death.

Haskin’s work on the Moon included many important discoveries, with the recognition of the Procellarum KREEP terrain as one of his final contributions. The IAU officially gave Haskin’s name to a farside crater on January 22, 2009, along with 18 other scientists, most Nobel Prize winners. The crater Haskin is a degraded 58-km-wide feature, about 10° degrees from the north pole.
